title: Steganography Image Encoder and Decoder
content:
Steganography image encoder and decoder This is a simple program in python which is used to encode the text in the the image and also used to decode the text from an image with the help of opencv and numpy library by usiing the Least Common Bit meathod (LSB).
GitHub: https://github.com/Tempest2488/Steganography-image-encoder-and-decoder
Requirements python v3.10 opencv-python v4.7.0 numpy v1.24.1 Usage of the Program Run the main.py script in the terminal. The script will prompt you to choose between three options:
Encode an image Decode an image Exit To encode the image to the file Choose the first option to encode the text in the file Enter the name along with the extention of the image file you want to encode (only PNG format is supported). Enter the text you want to encode in the image. The encoded image will be saved as original image file name + “_encoded.png” . To decode the text from an image Choose the second option to decode the text from the image Enter the name of the image file that you want to decode. The decoded text will be displayed in the terminal. Notes The encoding process stores the ASCII value of each character of the text in the least significant of the blue channel of the image’s pixels. The text encoding process may take some time for longer texts as the number of pixels needed to store the text increases with the length of the text. The image size must be large enough to store the text. If the image size is smaller than the length of the text, a “StopIteration” error will be raised.

title: Network Security Case Study: DesX Zolutions Ltd.
tags: network-security, network-design, cisco, vlsm, vlan, firewall, acl, aaa
content:
Case Brief I designed and implemented a secure network for a fictional company.
DesX Zolutions Ltd., a fast-growing architectural design firm that moved into a new office with ~160 employees/hosts. The company is expanding its digital operations and needed a structured, segmented network that supports operational efficiency and data protection.
Department Requirements (Summary) Design (55 hosts): Uses CAD/3D tools and cloud collaboration. Internet access plus Project Management; no access to HR, Finance, or IT. Project Management (40 hosts): Scheduling, resourcing, and client communication. Internet access plus Design and Finance; no access to HR or IT. HR (25 hosts): Recruitment and employee records. Internet access only; no access to other departments. Finance (30 hosts): Payroll, budgeting, invoicing, and reporting. Internet access plus Project Management; no access to HR, IT, or Design. IT (10 hosts): Maintains infrastructure and endpoints. Full access to all departments and servers. Shared Services and Access Web Server: Company website and internal web apps; accessible by all departments. DHCP Server: IP assignment for all subnets. Email Server: Internal and external communications for all departments. Conference Room: Shared video conferencing system for all departments. Solution Outline To present my solution and rationale, I structured the work into four phases:
Phase 1: Network Design and Planning
Requirements analysis, zone-of-trust segmentation, IP addressing with VLSM, topology selection, and justification. Phase 2: Network Implementation and Configuration
Device configuration, routing, DHCP, server services, wireless access, and simulated internet connectivity. Phase 3: Security Controls and Access Policies
AAA, ZPF, ACLs, and verification of allowed/blocked traffic. Phase 4: Critical Reflection and Evaluation
Security posture review, scalability, future-proofing, and implementation challenges. Phase 1: Network Design and Planning Overview of Organisation DesX Zolution is a rapidly growing architectural firm with approximately 160 employees, divided into five different departments. These departments are Design, Project Management, Finance, Human Resources (HR), and IT. Each department has a different role, which performs different business functions with different access network requirements for the departments within the company. To support these network requirements, a proper, secure and scalable network was designed using Cisco Packet Tracer, which focuses on confidentiality and proper utilisation of IP with the help of Variable Length Subnet Masking, which is also called VLSM.
Design Objectives Proper connectivity for all 160 hosts Segment each department to isolate traffic and improve security Ensure inter-department communication aligns with company policy Support dedicated servers (DHCP, Web, Email) Provide internet access via an external network Allow future expansion for users and servers Network Requirements Department Hosts Access Requirements Restrictions Design 55 Internet access and Project Management No access to HR, Finance, or IT Project Management 40 Internet access, Design, and Finance No access to IT Finance 30 Internet access and Project Management No access to HR, IT, or Design HR 25 Internet access only No access to other departments IT 10 Full access None Server 3 Full access None Conference 1 Full access None Zone of Trust Model To enhance the security and segmentation of the network, the design which is implemented follows the zone of trust model. Based on the network design, each zone represents a different trust level, which controls which information and packets flow in different departments and servers.
Zone Clients Trust Level Access Policy External ISP / Internet Low Untrusted network; traffic filtered at the router DMZ Web, Email, DHCP server Medium Accessible to internal users for services Internal - Business Design, Project Management, Finance High Subnets isolated to prevent unauthorized access Restricted Zone HR High Fully isolated from other business departments Administrative IT Very High Trusted IT zone for management and AAA Shared Access Zone Conference Room Medium Shared access for all departments IP Addressing and Subnetting Scheme I used the 192.168.10.0/24 private range with VLSM to allocate hosts efficiently and reduce IP waste.
Department Hosts Subnet Mask Prefix Usable Hosts Network ID First Host Last Host Broadcast Design 55 255.255.255.192 /26 62 192.168.10.0 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.62 192.168.10.63 Project Management 40 255.255.255.192 /26 62 192.168.10.64 192.168.10.65 192.168.10.126 192.168.10.127 Finance 30 255.255.255.224 /27 30 192.168.10.128 192.168.10.129 192.168.10.158 192.168.10.159 HR 25 255.255.255.224 /27 30 192.168.10.160 192.168.10.161 192.168.10.190 192.168.10.191 IT 10 255.255.255.240 /28 14 192.168.10.192 192.168.10.193 192.168.10.206 192.168.10.207 Server Room 3 255.255.255.248 /29 6 192.168.10.208 192.168.10.209 192.168.10.214 192.168.10.215 Conference 1 255.255.255.252 /30 2 192.168.10.216 192.168.10.217 192.168.10.218 192.168.10.219 I connected each department to its own access switch, and uplinked those to the Layer 3 core switch. Physical Network Design I designed a hierarchical star architecture with three layers (core, distribution, access) to improve scalability, segmentation, and management. At the core layer, I used a Layer 3 switch as the central distribution device to maintain VLANs and forward traffic. I connected the core router to the ISP router and used it for inter-VLAN routing, DHCP relay, and security controls (ZPF and ACLs).
Network Topology I used a hierarchical star topology in Cisco Packet Tracer with two routers, one Layer 3 switch, and seven Layer 2 switches. I configured the first router as the simulated ISP (external network). I configured the core router to serve as the main internet gateway and firewall, and connected it directly to the ISP router. I trunked the Layer 3 switch to the core router to distribute traffic to each Layer 2 switch. I connected each Layer 2 switch to end hosts and servers within its subnet.
Justification of using the network topology Topology Selection I chose a two-tier design instead of a three-tier model to reduce complexity and cost. With fewer than 200 hosts, this topology provides strong performance and manageable operations.
Star Topology Selection This star arrangement allows me to add new departments by connecting additional access switches to the core, while keeping routing and security policies centralized.
Segmentation Strategy I achieved segmentation using IP-based subnetting with VLSM. Each department operates in its own subnet and is connected to the dedicated layer 2 switch of that department, which helps in physical and logical isolation. This also helps in reducing broadcast traffic and simplifying troubleshooting.
Security Implementation I used a defense-in-depth model that combines the Zone-Based Policy Firewall (ZPF) and Access Control Lists (ACLs) I configured the core router to enforce ZPF rules, which allow only required services such as HTTP, DNS and ICMP. I also implemented ACLs on the core router, which provide additional granular filtering inside the LAN Network I configured AAA (Authentication, Authorisation, and Accounting) on each device, which secures administrative login and records configuration.
Security And Functional Benefits This design allows efficient performance due to the inter-subnet routing and reduced broadcast traffic; it also ensures scalability by allowing expansion of the network with new subnets. It provides multi-layer security with the help of ZPF, ACLs and AAA and maintains compliance by isolating each department in accordance with the GDPR and Financial Data Protection Act.
Phase 2: Network Implementation and Configuration In this phase, I focused on configuring the network devices according to the proposed topology and testing connectivity between internal departments and the simulated external internet.
Configuring the ISP router In Cisco Packet Tracer, I configured the ISP router to simulate the internet. The router was assigned an external IP address 8.10.1.254, which provides connectivity to the core router. I also added a static route back to the internal network via the core router.
I also configured a loopback address on the ISP router to emulate an external server and test internet reachability.
Core Router Configuration I used a 4331 Cisco router as the core router to connect the external internet to the internal network. It handles inter-department routing, DHCP relay, and security controls. I trunked it to the Layer 3 switch, created sub-interfaces per VLAN to serve as default gateways, and added a static return route to the ISP. I configured the ISP-facing IP address on the core router and changed the hostname.
I trunked the core router to the Layer 3 switch.
I configured sub-interfaces (for example, VLAN 10 for Design). The same pattern applies to VLANs 20, 30, and so on.
Configuring the static routing in the Core router to the ISP router I configured DHCP relay on the core router to provide IP addresses to internal hosts.
I verified core router interfaces with show ip interface brief.
I checked routing with show ip route and confirmed the static route was set.
I verified connectivity by pinging from the core router to the ISP router.
Layer 3 Switch Configuration I configured the Layer 3 switch as the main distribution point between the core router and the Layer 2 access switches. All the VLANs from VLAN 10 to VLAN 70 were created in the layer 3 switch, and it was stored in the VLAN database. I configured the uplink to the core router as a trunk using 802.1Q encapsulation. I configured the Layer 3 switch to perform only Layer 2 functions, like not having IP routing or not having any SVIs or Switched Virtual Interfaces. All routing is handled by the core router using a router-on-a-stick design. I verified this using show vlan brief and show interface trunk. I configured the VLAN for a layer 3 switch
Configuring the TRUNK PORT TO COREROUTER I configured access ports on the Layer 2 switch. Note that after testing the spanning tree, portfast has been disabled
I verified the VLANs using show vlan brief.
I verified the trunk using show interface trunk.
I checked interface status using show interface status.
Layer 2 Access Switch Configuration I used seven Layer 2 switches to connect end devices to the access layer. I assigned each switch to its department VLAN and mapped ports to the correct subnet. VLAN 10 – Design (Design-SW) VLAN 20 – Project Management (PM-SW) VLAN 30 – Finance (Finance-SW) VLAN 40 – Human Resources (HR-SW) VLAN 50 – IT (IT-SW) VLAN 60 – Servers (Server-SW) VLAN 70 – Conference (Conference-SW) I configured each Layer 2 switch for its departmental VLAN and connected PCs, wireless access points, and other devices. The same command patterns apply to all switches when mapped to the correct VLAN.
Creating a VLAN for project management I configured access ports for Project Management PCs.
I verified the configuration using show running-config.
DHCP Server Configuration I deployed a dedicated DHCP server in VLAN 60 with the static IP 192.168.10.210/29, default gateway 192.168.10.209, and DNS 8.8.8.8. I created seven DHCP pools (one per VLAN) to provide automatic IPs with the correct subnet mask, gateway, and DNS values based on the subnetting plan. Design Pool (VLAN 10): 192.168.10.0/26 and the Gateway 192.168.10.1 Project Management Pool (VLAN 20): 192.168.10.64/26, and the Gateway is 192.168.10.65 Finance Pool (VLAN 30): 192.168.10.128/27 and the Gateway is 192.168.10.129 HR Pool (VLAN 40): 192.168.10.160/27 and the Gateway is 192.168.10.161 IT Pool (VLAN 50): 192.168.10.192/28, and the Gateway is 192.168.10.193 Conference Pool (VLAN 70): 192.168.10.216/30, and the Gateway is 192.168.10.217 The server VLAN (VLAN 60) has no DHCP pool because servers are statically addressed. I configured the core router as the DHCP relay to forward broadcast requests from hosts and access points to the DHCP server using ip helper-address 192.168.10.210.
Configuring a static IP for the DHCP server Configuring the DHCP Pool using the subnetting table for each department IP address received using DHCP for PC 2 in Project Management
Web Server Configuration I configured the web server in VLAN 60 with the static IP address 192.168.10.211/29.
I enabled HTTP and HTTPS services.
I added a custom landing page for the internal site.
I validated access by loading the server IP from a client.
Email Server Configuration I configured the email server with the static IP 192.168.10.212 and set the domain to desxzolution.com.
I applied the static addressing and service settings.
I configured email accounts on each PC; the following is an example of a Design user.
To validate delivery, I created the local account on the Project Management PC and sent a test message from Design.
I sent a test email from Design to Project Management.
Email accounts used:
Department Email Accounts Design design1@desxzolutions.com, design2@desxzolutions.com Project Management pm1@desxzolutions.com, pm2@desxzolutions.com Finance finance1@desxzolutions.com, finance2@desxzolutions.com HR hr1@desxzolutions.com, hr2@desxzolutions.com IT it1@desxzolutions.com, it2@desxzolutions.com Conference conference1@desxzolutions.com All email accounts use the same password: cisco123.
Wireless Access Points Configuration I configured one WPA2-secured access point per department with a unique SSID and password.
I set the HR access point password.
I connected the HR wireless laptop to the HR access point.
I verified the connection to the HR access point.
I confirmed the laptop received an IP via DHCP through the HR access point.
Access point configuration:
AP Location IP (example) SSID Password VLAN Design-AP Design-SW 192.168.10.5 DesX-Design Design@2025! 10 PM-AP PM-SW 192.168.10.70 DesX-PM PM@2025! 20 Finance-AP Finance-SW 192.168.10.135 DesX-Finance Finance@2025! 30 HR-AP HR-SW 192.168.10.165 DesX-HR HR@2025! 40 IT-AP IT-SW 192.168.10.195 DesX-IT IT@2025! 50 Server-AP Server-SW 192.168.10.213 DesX-Servers Servers@2025! 60 Conference-AP Conference 192.168.10.218 DesX-Conference Conf@2025! 70 Verifying Simulated Internet Connectivity I set the default route on the core router toward the ISP.
I set the return route on the ISP router back to internal networks.
I verified connectivity by pinging from a Design PC to the ISP using the static IP and loopback address.
I repeated the same test from Project Management.
Phase 3: Security Controls and Access Policies Zone-Based Policy Firewall (ZPF) I configured a Zone-Based Policy Firewall on the core router to inspect and enforce security policies. I grouped all internal VLANs into one internal zone and the ISP into an external zone. This approach works around Packet Tracer limitations with ZPF and VLAN sub-interfaces while still enforcing boundary controls.
I defined the security zones.
I verified zone definitions with show security zone.
I assigned interfaces to the zones.
I created class maps.
I created and applied the policies.
I created the zone pair to allow internal clients to access the internet.
I finalized interface assignments for internal and external zones.
Access Control Lists (ACLs) I implemented extended ACLs on the core router to enforce inter-department access rules and protect internal resources. I created seven ACLs (one per VLAN) and placed DHCP permits at the top of each list to allow essential services while blocking restricted traffic.
I configured the Design VLAN ACL.
I applied each ACL to its corresponding sub-interface.
I verified the ACLs with show ip access-lists.
I validated allowed traffic by pinging from Design to Project Management.
I validated blocked traffic by pinging from Design to HR.
AAA Configuration I configured AAA on all devices (ISP router, core router, and all Layer 2 switches) to secure administrative access.
Username: admin / Password: Admin123! Enable password: Enable123! Backup user: backup / Password: Backup123! I applied AAA settings and console/VTY hardening on the core router.
I validated access from a client and a remote session to the core router.
Phase 4: Critical Reflection and Evaluation Security Evaluation I evaluated the design against confidentiality, integrity, and availability goals for a ~160-host organization. The result is a layered, segmented network with enforced access controls and authenticated administration.
Key Strengths VLAN segmentation: Each department operates in its own VLAN, isolating traffic. ACL enforcement: Extended ACLs on all seven sub-interfaces enforce inter-department rules. AAA hardening: Administrative access is authenticated and audited. Wireless security: WPA2-PSK secures departmental access points. Least privilege: HR is isolated for compliance, Finance can reach only Project Management, Design cannot reach Finance, and IT retains administrative access. Weaknesses Single point of failure: The core router handles routing and firewall duties; a failure would disrupt most services. Limited logging: No centralized logging or SIEM integration was configured. Insecure management protocol: Telnet exposes credentials in plaintext. Scalability and Future-Proofing The design supports moderate growth but will hit limits due to IP exhaustion and the standalone core router.
Current utilization
Design VLAN has limited remaining capacity. Conference VLAN is fully utilized. Only 36 addresses remain from 192.168.10.220 onward. Short-term growth
Supportable up to ~200–250 users by adding VLANs. Long-term constraints (~300 users)
Router-on-a-stick becomes a bottleneck. The /24 address space will be exhausted. Future-proofing steps
Migrate to Layer 3 switching with SVIs for inter-VLAN routing. Expand address space for larger subnets and flexibility. Add a backup router for resiliency. Consider a Zero Trust model for centralized policy enforcement. Challenges and How I Addressed Them ZPF limitation in Packet Tracer: ZPF rejected sub-interface zone membership. I placed all VLANs into a single internal zone and enforced inter-department controls with ACLs. DHCP relay across VLANs: DHCP broadcasts initially failed. I added ip helper-address to all sub-interfaces to relay DHCP to the server.

title: Realtek Driver Updater
content:
Realtek Driver Updates Without the Busywork I got tired of manually pulling from git, running make, and then installing with sudo make install every time I needed to rebuild the rtw88 driver. I wanted something cleaner — a one-stop GUI to handle the whole process with a few button clicks.
This is where my project comes in: Realtek Updater — a Python-based GUI tool that wraps the entire update cycle for the Realtek rtw88 driver.
Repo: https://github.com/Tempest2488/Realtek-Updater
What It Does Realtek Updater wraps the classic git pull, make, and sudo make install commands into a neat interface using tkinter. You launch it with sudo, hit a button, and it runs the full update cycle.
It:
Runs all commands inside a defined working directory (hardcoded in this case) Streams all output in real time inside a log window Prevents you from accidentally launching it without sudo Keeps the interface dead simple — just 3 buttons and a log window Features Real-time terminal output displayed in a scrollable textbox. Buttons for Git Pull, Make, and Sudo Make Install. Threaded command execution — the GUI doesn’t freeze while it runs. Verifies that you’ve launched it with sudo before anything even loads. Hardcoded working directory:
~/src/rtw88 — change it to match your local driver path. Requirements Requirement Description Python 3.x Core language for running the script tkinter GUI library (comes pre-installed with Python) sudo access Required to execute make install properly Installation Clone the repo and install dependencies (there are no extras beyond Python):
git clone https://github.com/Tempest2488/Realtek-Updater cd Realtek-Updater Then launch it like this:
sudo python3 gui.py A Quick Look at the Code The core logic lives in a class called GitMakeInstaller. The general flow:
On startup, the app checks if it’s run as root using os.geteuid(). There’s a working directory defined at the top. This is where all the commands run from. Each button is wired to run a shell command using subprocess.Popen(). Output is streamed line by line into a ScrolledText widget. Everything runs on separate threads so the GUI stays responsive. Example method:
def run_command(self, command):
Runs the command in a thread, logs output in real time, and shows a message box if something goes wrong.
def check_sudo(self):
Makes sure you’re running as sudo. If not, it shows an error and exits.
The GUI layout is dead simple — just one row of buttons and a big log output box underneath.
Final Thoughts This wasn’t built to be flashy. It was built to get the job done. If you regularly pull and build kernel modules or driver sources, this will save you time and reduce mistakes.
You can always tweak the working directory or add buttons for clean builds, tests, or custom scripts. But even in this minimal state, it already saves me time — and that is exactly why I built it.

title: Return Oriented Programming
content:
ROP Exploit with Arbitrary Write to .bss and Reverse Shell via system() Description: This repository contains a Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) exploit targeting a 64-bit Linux binary vulnerable to buffer overflow. The exploit performs an arbitrary write to the .bss section to inject a reverse shell command, which is then executed using system(). The goal is to gain a remote shell on the target system.
This repository contains an exploit for a 64-bit Linux binary vulnerable to a buffer overflow.
The exploit uses ROP (Return-Oriented Programming) to achieve a write-what-where primitive, injecting a reverse shell command into the .bss section and then calling system() to execute it.
The exploit is written in Python using the Pwntools library.
GitHub: https://github.com/Tempest2488/ROP-exploit-bss-reverse-shell
Contents remote_solve.py – Exploit script (writes reverse shell to .bss and executes it) target – Target binary (64-bit ELF) remote_libc.so.6 – Remote libc used by the server Vulnerability Summary Binary: target Architecture: x86_64 Protections: NX enabled, no PIE, no stack canary Vulnerability: Classic buffer overflow with arbitrary memory write Technique: Use ROP chain to write a reverse shell command into .bss memory Call system() on that command Use exit() to gracefully terminate (optional) Requirements Python 3.6+ Pwntools: pip install pwntools Ngrok: Used to create a TCP tunnel from the remote machine back to your local listener
To run Ngrok for this exploit, use: ngrok tcp 4444 Notes The payload uses custom ROP gadgets to write arbitrary data into memory. This technique avoids relying on already present command strings in memory. Also, the code will print out important base addresses of functions such as: offset system bin_sh libc base address Initially, I attempted to use the generic SSH client approach to execute the exploit remotely.
However, I wasn’t able to get a reverse shell this way.
Instead, I successfully established a reverse shell by creating a TCP tunnel using Ngrok to expose port 4444 on my local machine.
Demonstration First, make sure you have the correct Libc since if the machine turns off or restarts, then the libc base address will change due to ASLR. So you have to go through the whole phase 2 again to find the libc base address. You have to add the base address here in the code. Don’t save the file yet in the terminal and run ngrok tcp 4444 Once you run the code, you will be able to see this. Take the username and port given in ngrok; in this case, I highlighted and then put in the code in the username and port sections, respectively Once this part is done, save the file and run it. It will pack the payload into a file called payload.txt. Then, run a netcat listener to be able to receive the reverse shell. The command is nc -lnvp 4444 Once the listener is running, take the payload.txt and upload it to the upload solutions on the webpage Once you submit, you see a message saying BAD. Go to the terminal where your netcat is listening for incoming connections. You will see that I have caught the connection Disclaimer This project is intended for educational purposes only.
Unauthorized access to computer systems is illegal and unethical.
By using this code, you agree that:
You are testing in a controlled, authorized environment. You take full responsibility for your actions. The author(s) are not liable for any misuse or damage caused. Always practice responsible disclosure and ethical hacking.

title: Hash-Cracker
content:
Hash-Cracker I built a small, simple program that can crack SHA-256 hashes using a wordlist. It supports two workflows: pass a CSV of hashes or enter a single hash interactively. I’ll keep making commits if I change anything.
GitHub: https://github.com/Tempest2488/Hashcracker
What it Does Cracks SHA-256 hashes using a wordlist Supports CSV input (list.csv) for batch cracking Supports interactive mode for a single hash Prints start/end timestamps and the cracked password when found Requirements Python 3.x colorama Usage Option 1: CSV Mode Run the script with a CSV file of hashes:
python3 main.py list.csv Option 2: Interactive Mode Run the script without arguments and paste a single hash when prompted:
python3 main.py How It Works (Quick Summary) The program reads a wordlist (THE PASSWORD.txt), hashes each candidate with SHA-256, and compares it to the provided hash (or each hash in list.csv). When it matches, it prints the plaintext password and exits.
main.py import csv import hashlib from colorama import Fore from datetime import datetime import sys print(Fore.BLUE + """dP dP dP a88888b. dP 88 88 88 d8' `88 88 88aaaaa88a .d8888b. .d8888b. 88d888b. 88 88d888b. .d8888b. .d8888b. 88 .dP .d8888b. 88d888b. 88 88 88' `88 Y8ooooo. 88' `88 88 88' `88 88' `88 88' `"" 88888" 88ooood8 88' `88 88 88 88. .88 88 88 88 Y8. .88 88 88. .88 88. ... 88 `8b. 88. ... 88 dP dP `88888P8 `88888P' dP dP Y88888P' dP `88888P8 `88888P' dP `YP `88888P' dP ooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooo """) print(Fore.RED + """By Talen Neil Serrao""" + Fore.RESET) try: if sys.argv[1] == "list.csv" or './list.csv': current_time = datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S") print( Fore.LIGHTWHITE_EX + "[i] " + Fore.LIGHTMAGENTA_EX + "Cracking started: " + Fore.LIGHTWHITE_EX + current_time + '\n' + Fore.RESET) wordlist = bytes(open("THE PASSWORD.txt").read(), 'utf-8') with open('list.csv', 'r') as read_obj: csv_reader = csv.reader(read_obj) for row in csv_reader: for passw in wordlist.split(): hashed = hashlib.sha256(passw).hexdigest() if hashed == row[0]: print(Fore.LIGHTGREEN_EX + "the hash you have given is cracked") print(Fore.LIGHTBLUE_EX + "the password is", passw.decode('utf-8')) print(Fore.YELLOW + "Your hash is", row) print(Fore.LIGHTMAGENTA_EX + "\nCracking ended: ", current_time + '\n' + Fore.RESET) pass elif hashed != row[0]: pass except IndexError as e: hash256 = input(Fore.LIGHTYELLOW_EX + "Enter the hash password: ") current_time = datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S") print( Fore.LIGHTWHITE_EX + "[i] " + Fore.LIGHTMAGENTA_EX + "Cracking started: " + Fore.LIGHTWHITE_EX + current_time + '\n' + Fore.RESET) wordlist = bytes(open("THE PASSWORD.txt").read(), 'utf-8') for passw passw.decode('utf-8')) print(Fore.YELLOW + "Your hash is", hash256) print(Fore.LIGHTMAGENTA_EX + "\nCracking ended: ", current_time + '\n' + Fore.RESET) quit() elif hashed != hash256: pass #
